title: 03 — Azure DevOps in Depth
html:
03 — Azure DevOps in Depth

Still the dominant CI/CD platform in enterprise .NET shops. This file covers YAML Pipelines properly, plus Repos, Artifacts, Boards, and how it compares to GitHub Actions.

1. The five services

Service What it is Notes
Repos Git hosting Branch policies are the important part
Pipelines CI/CD YAML pipelines (current) vs Classic (legacy UI — avoid for new work)
Artifacts Package feeds NuGet, npm, Maven, Python, Universal Packages
Boards Work tracking Links commits/PRs/builds to work items — the audit trail enterprises want
Test Plans Manual test management Separately licensed; rarely used by dev teams

Hierarchy: Organisation (dev.azure.com/myorg) → Project → Repos / Pipelines / Feeds. Permissions and service connections are scoped at the project level, which matters for isolating production credentials.

2. YAML pipeline structure

Pipeline
└── Stages          (sequential by default; deployment gates live here)
    └── Jobs        (parallel by default; each on its own agent)
        └── Steps   (sequential; task or script)

trigger:
  branches:
    include: [main, release/*]
  paths:
    exclude: ['**/*', 'docs/*']

pr:
  branches:
    include: [main]
  # `pr: none` disables PR validation for this pipeline

schedules:
  - cron: '0 2 * * 1-5'          # UTC
    displayName: Nightly build
    branches: { include: [main] }
    always: true                  # run even if there were no code changes

variables:
  - name: buildConfiguration
    value: Release
  - group: shared-nonsecret-vars  # a variable group from the Library
  - template: vars/common.yml     # variables from a template file

pool:
  vmImage: ubuntu-latest

stages:
  - stage: Build
    jobs:
      - job: BuildApi
        steps:
          - checkout: self
            fetchDepth: 0
          - task: UseDotNet@2
            inputs: { packageType: sdk, version: '10.0.x' }
          - script: dotnet build -c $(buildConfiguration)
            displayName: Build

  - stage: DeployDev
    dependsOn: Build
    condition: and(succeeded(), eq(variables['Build.SourceBranch'], 'refs/heads/main'))
    jobs:
      - deployment: DeployApi        # ← a DEPLOYMENT job, not a regular job
        environment: dev             # ← unlocks approvals, checks, and history
        strategy:
          runOnce:
            deploy:
              steps:
                - download: current
                  artifact: api
                - task: AzureWebApp@1
                  inputs: { azureSubscription: 'sc-azure-dev', appName: 'app-myapi-dev' }

2.1 job vs deployment — the distinction that matters

job deployment
Purpose Build, test, general work Deploy to an environment
Gets A plain agent Environment history, approvals, checks, resource targeting
Artifacts Must download explicitly Auto-downloads all pipeline artifacts (unless you say otherwise)
Strategies — runOnce, rolling, canary

💡 Always use deployment jobs for deployments. You get the approval gates, a per-environment deployment history, and traceability from work item → commit → build → deployment, which is exactly what enterprise change management asks for.

# Deployment strategies
strategy:
  runOnce:
    preDeploy:  { steps: [...] }   # e.g. take out of rotation
    deploy:     { steps: [...] }
    routeTraffic:{ steps: [...] }  # e.g. slot swap
    postRouteTraffic: { steps: [...] }  # e.g. smoke tests + monitoring window
    on:
      failure: { steps: [...] }    # ← rollback goes here
      success: { steps: [...] }

The postRouteTraffic + on.failure pair is the built-in place for verify-then-rollback, and most teams never use it.

3. ⭐ Service connections and workload identity federation

A service connection is how a pipeline authenticates to Azure (or a registry, or GitHub).

3.1 Use Workload Identity Federation — not a secret

sequenceDiagram
    participant P as Azure Pipelines job
    participant D as Azure DevOps OIDC issuer
    participant E as Microsoft Entra ID
    participant A as Azure resources
    P->>D: request a token for the service connection
    D-->>P: JWT with sub = sc://myorg/myproject/sc-azure-prod
    P->>E: exchange it
    E->>E: match against the federated credential<br/>on the app registration / user-assigned managed identity
    E-->>P: short-lived Azure access token
    P->>A: deploy

Why: no client secret to expire (the classic Monday-morning outage: "the pipeline broke and nobody changed anything" — the service principal secret hit its two-year expiry), nothing to rotate, nothing to leak.

Setup:

  • In the service connection creation dialog, choose Azure Resource Manager → Workload Identity federation (automatic). Azure DevOps creates the app registration and federated credential for you.
  • 💡 Manual mode with a user-assigned managed identity is the recommended target for production: you control the identity, its lifecycle, and its RBAC independently of the DevOps project.
  • ⚠️ The subject claim format is sc://<org>/<project>/<connection-name>. Get it wrong and authentication fails silently or with an unhelpful error. If you rename the service connection, the claim changes and the credential must be updated.
  • Existing secret-based connections can be converted in place if Azure DevOps originally created them — there's a "Convert" action on the connection.
# Manual setup against a user-assigned managed identity
az identity federated-credential create \
  --name "azdo-prod" \
  --identity-name "id-pipeline-prod" \
  --resource-group "rg-identity" \
  --issuer "https://vstoken.dev.azure.com/<organisation-id>" \
  --subject "sc://myorg/myproject/sc-azure-prod" \
  --audiences "api://AzureADTokenExchange"

3.2 Locking service connections down

Control Effect
Restrict to specific pipelines (uncheck "Grant access to all pipelines") A new pipeline can't deploy to production without an explicit grant
Approvals and Checks on the connection A human gate at the credential, not just the environment — belt and braces
Branch control check Only main/refs/tags/* may use this connection
Separate connections per environment A dev pipeline compromise cannot reach production
Narrow RBAC scope Grant at the resource-group scope, not the subscription

⚠️ The most common Azure DevOps security hole: one Contributor-at-subscription-scope service connection, shared by every pipeline in the project, with "grant access to all pipelines" ticked. Any developer who can create a pipeline can then do anything in the subscription.

4. Variables, variable groups, and secrets

variables:
  - name: buildConfiguration          # plain pipeline variable
    value: Release
  - group: myapp-prod-secrets         # variable group from Library (can be Key Vault-backed)
  - name: computed
    value: $[ format('{0}-{1}', variables.buildConfiguration, variables['Build.BuildId']) ]

Three syntaxes, and the difference is a common interview question:

Syntax Resolved Use
${{ }} Compile time (template expansion, before the run) Template logic, ${{ if }}, ${{ each }}
$[ ] Runtime, before the job starts Setting a variable from an expression, dependency conditions
$( ) Runtime, inside the step Normal variable usage in scripts and task inputs 
# Setting a variable from a script for later steps/jobs
- script: echo "##vso[task.setvariable variable=version;isOutput=true]1.4.$(Build.BuildId)"
  name: setVersion

# Consuming it in a later JOB
- job: Deploy
  dependsOn: Build
  variables:
    version: $[ dependencies.Build.outputs['setVersion.version'] ]

Secrets:

  • Mark a variable as secret → it's masked in logs and not exposed as an environment variable automatically. You must map it explicitly:
- script: ./deploy.sh
  env:
    API_KEY: $(myApiKey)        # ⚠️ required — secret vars are NOT auto-injected into env
  • 💡 Key Vault-backed variable groups are better than storing secrets in Azure DevOps: the secret lives in Key Vault, is audited there, and rotation happens in one place.
  • ⚠️ Secrets are still visible to anyone who can edit the pipeline (they can echo a transformed version). Least privilege on pipeline edit rights is part of your secret management.

5. Templates — the reuse mechanism

# templates/build-dotnet.yml
parameters:
  - name: projectPath
    type: string
  - name: dotnetVersion
    type: string
    default: '10.0.x'
  - name: runIntegrationTests
    type: boolean
    default: true

steps:
  - task: UseDotNet@2
    inputs: { packageType: sdk, version: ${{ parameters.dotnetVersion }} }

  - task: Cache@2
    inputs:
      key: 'nuget | "$(Agent.OS)" | **/packages.lock.json'
      restoreKeys: 'nuget | "$(Agent.OS)"'
      path: $(NUGET_PACKAGES)

  - script: dotnet restore --locked-mode
    displayName: Restore

  - script: dotnet build ${{ parameters.projectPath }} -c Release --no-restore -warnaserror
    displayName: Build

  - script: dotnet test --no-build -c Release --logger trx --collect:"XPlat Code Coverage"
    displayName: Unit tests

  - ${{ if eq(parameters.runIntegrationTests, true) }}:
    - script: dotnet test --no-build -c Release --filter Category=Integration
      displayName: Integration tests

# Using it
steps:
  - template: templates/build-dotnet.yml
    parameters:
      projectPath: src/Api/Api.csproj
      runIntegrationTests: false

Template types: steps, jobs, stages, and variables templates. Templates can live in another repository:

resources:
  repositories:
    - repository: templates
      type: git
      name: Platform/pipeline-templates
      ref: refs/tags/v2.1.0            # 💡 pin to a tag

stages:
  - template: stages/build-deploy.yml@templates
    parameters: { serviceName: myapi }

💡 Required templates as a security control: an organisation can enforce that every pipeline extends an approved base template, guaranteeing that security scans and approval gates cannot be bypassed by a team writing its own YAML.

extends:
  template: security-baseline.yml@templates
  parameters:
    stages: [...]         # your stages are injected into the enforced skeleton

6. Environments, approvals, and checks

Environments (Pipelines → Environments) are the deployment-target abstraction. Attach:

Check Purpose
Approvals Named approvers must sign off; you can require multiple, and forbid the requester from approving their own
Branch control Only main or a tag may deploy here
Business hours Block deployments outside a window
Exclusive lock Serialise deployments to this environment
Invoke REST API / Azure Function Custom gate — e.g. "is there an active incident?", "is the change ticket approved?"
Query Azure Monitor alerts 💡 Block the deploy if an alert is firing. Underused and excellent
Evaluate artifact Policy-as-code on the artifact (e.g. image scanned, signed)

An environment can also have resources (Kubernetes namespaces, VMs), which gives per-resource deployment history and lets you target them in a deployment job.

7. Full production pipeline: .NET + Angular → Azure

name: $(Date:yyyyMMdd).$(Rev:r)

trigger:
  branches: { include: [main] }
  paths: { exclude: ['**/*', 'docs/*'] }

pr:
  branches: { include: [main] }

resources:
  repositories:
    - repository: templates
      type: git
      name: Platform/pipeline-templates
      ref: refs/tags/v2.1.0

variables:
  - name: buildConfiguration
    value: Release
  - name: version
    value: '1.4.$(Build.BuildId)'
  - name: artifactName
    value: 'api'

stages:
# ═══════════════════════════ BUILD ═══════════════════════════
- stage: Build
  jobs:
  - job: Backend
    pool: { vmImage: ubuntu-latest }
    steps:
      - checkout: self
        fetchDepth: 0

      - template: steps/build-dotnet.yml@templates
        parameters: { projectPath: src/Api/Api.csproj }

      - task: PublishTestResults@2
        condition: succeededOrFailed()        # publish even when tests fail
        inputs:
          testResultsFormat: VSTest
          testResultsFiles: '**/*.trx'
          failTaskOnFailedTests: true

      - task: PublishCodeCoverageResults@2
        inputs: { summaryFileLocation: '**/coverage.cobertura.xml' }

      - script: >
          dotnet publish src/Api/Api.csproj -c $(buildConfiguration)
          -o $(Build.ArtifactStagingDirectory)/api --no-build /p:Version=$(version)
        displayName: Publish

      - publish: $(Build.ArtifactStagingDirectory)/api
        artifact: $(artifactName)

  - job: Frontend
    pool: { vmImage: ubuntu-latest }
    steps:
      - task: NodeTool@0
        inputs: { versionSpec: '22.x' }
      - task: Cache@2
        inputs:
          key: 'npm | "$(Agent.OS)" | ClientApp/package-lock.json'
          path: $(Pipeline.Workspace)/.npm
      - script: npm ci --cache $(Pipeline.Workspace)/.npm
        workingDirectory: ClientApp
      - script: npm run lint && npm run test -- --watch=false --browsers=ChromeHeadless
        workingDirectory: ClientApp
      - script: npm run build -- --configuration production
        workingDirectory: ClientApp
      - publish: ClientApp/dist/browser
        artifact: web

  - job: Security
    pool: { vmImage: ubuntu-latest }
    steps:
      - script: |
          dotnet list package --vulnerable --include-transitive 2>&1 | tee out.txt
          ! grep -q "has the following vulnerable packages" out.txt
        displayName: Vulnerable dependency check
      - task: CredScan@3         # or Microsoft Security DevOps extension
      - task: MicrosoftSecurityDevOps@1

# ═══════════════════════════ DEV ═══════════════════════════
- stage: DeployDev
  dependsOn: Build
  condition: and(succeeded(), eq(variables['Build.SourceBranch'], 'refs/heads/main'))
  jobs:
  - deployment: Dev
    environment: dev
    pool: { vmImage: ubuntu-latest }
    strategy:
      runOnce:
        deploy:
          steps:
            - task: AzureCLI@2
              displayName: Apply database migrations
              inputs:
                azureSubscription: sc-azure-dev
                scriptType: bash
                scriptLocation: inlineScript
                inlineScript: |
                  dotnet tool install --global dotnet-ef
                  dotnet ef database update --project src/Infrastructure --startup-project src/Api

            - task: AzureWebApp@1
              inputs:
                azureSubscription: sc-azure-dev
                appName: app-myapi-dev
                package: $(Pipeline.Workspace)/$(artifactName)
                deploymentMethod: zipDeploy

            - script: curl -fsS https://app-myapi-dev.azurewebsites.net/health/ready
              displayName: Smoke test

# ═══════════════════════════ PRODUCTION ═══════════════════════════
- stage: DeployProd
  dependsOn: DeployDev
  jobs:
  - deployment: Prod
    environment: production          # ← approvals and checks configured here
    pool: { vmImage: ubuntu-latest }
    strategy:
      runOnce:
        deploy:
          steps:
            - task: AzureWebApp@1
              displayName: Deploy to the staging slot
              inputs:
                azureSubscription: sc-azure-prod
                appName: app-myapi-prod
                deployToSlotOrASE: true
                resourceGroupName: rg-myapp-prod
                slotName: staging
                package: $(Pipeline.Workspace)/$(artifactName)

            - script: |
                for i in {1..30}; do
                  code=$(curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" \
                    https://app-myapi-prod-staging.azurewebsites.net/health/ready)
                  [ "$code" = "200" ] && exit 0
                  sleep 5
                done
                exit 1
              displayName: Wait for the staging slot to be healthy

        routeTraffic:
          steps:
            - task: AzureAppServiceManage@0
              inputs:
                azureSubscription: sc-azure-prod
                resourceGroupName: rg-myapp-prod
                webAppName: app-myapi-prod
                sourceSlot: staging
                action: 'Swap Slots'

        postRouteTraffic:
          steps:
            - script: |
                sleep 30
                curl -fsS https://api.example.com/health/ready
              displayName: Verify production

        on:
          failure:
            steps:
              - task: AzureAppServiceManage@0
                displayName: Roll back (swap again)
                inputs:
                  azureSubscription: sc-azure-prod
                  resourceGroupName: rg-myapp-prod
                  webAppName: app-myapi-prod
                  sourceSlot: staging
                  action: 'Swap Slots'

8. Azure Repos — branch policies

Configure per branch (Repos → Branches → Branch policies). The ones that matter:

Policy Why
Minimum number of reviewers Usually 1–2; enable "reset votes on new changes"
Check for linked work items The traceability enterprises require
Check for comment resolution Stops merges with unaddressed feedback
Build validation ⭐ The PR pipeline must pass. Set it to required and set an expiry
Status checks External tools (SonarQube, security scanners)
Automatically included reviewers Path-based ownership (the equivalent of CODEOWNERS)
Limit merge types 💡 Squash-only gives a clean, bisectable history
Require branches to be up to date Catches semantic conflicts before merge

⚠️ Watch who has "Bypass policies when completing pull requests". It's frequently granted broadly and quietly defeats every policy above.

9. Azure Artifacts

Private package feeds for NuGet, npm, Maven, Python, and Universal Packages.

<!-- nuget.config -->
<packageSources>
  <clear />
  <add key="internal" value="https://pkgs.dev.azure.com/myorg/_packaging/internal/nuget/v3/index.json" />
  <add key="nuget.org" value="https://api.nuget.org/v3/index.json" />
</packageSources>

- task: NuGetAuthenticate@1        # authenticates the agent to the feed
- script: dotnet restore

Concepts to know:

  • Upstream sources: the feed proxies and caches nuget.org, so you get resilience against upstream outages and a record of every package used.
  • Views (@local, @prerelease, @release): promote a package through quality gates.
  • Retention policies: prune old versions, but ⚠️ never delete a version something still depends on.

⚠️ Dependency confusion attack: if your internal package name also exists on nuget.org, a resolver configured with both sources may pull the public one. Mitigations: <clear /> plus explicit sources, upstream sources with a reserved prefix, or package source mapping in nuget.config.

10. Agents and pools

Pool Notes
Microsoft-hosted Fresh VM per job, clean state, a broad software image. Parallel jobs are purchased
Self-hosted Your machine/VM/container. Needed for private network access, special tooling, or licensing. You own patching and cleanup
Scale set agents Self-hosted on a VMSS that Azure DevOps scales — a good middle ground
Managed DevOps Pools 🔄 Newer managed offering combining hosted convenience with VNet integration

⚠️ Self-hosted agents accumulate state. A build passing because of a leftover file from a previous run is a genuinely nasty failure mode. Use containerised jobs or clean the workspace:

jobs:
  - job: Build
    workspace: { clean: all }

💡 For private-endpoint Azure resources (an App Service with public access disabled, a private SQL), you need an agent inside the VNet — a scale-set agent or a self-hosted agent on an Azure VM.

11. Azure DevOps vs GitHub Actions

Azure DevOps GitHub Actions
Model Stages/jobs/steps; strong deployment semantics Workflows/jobs/steps; simpler model
Deployment gates ⭐ Rich: approvals, business hours, Azure Monitor checks, REST gates, exclusive locks Environments with reviewers, wait timers, branch rules
Reuse Templates (steps/jobs/stages/variables), required templates for governance Reusable workflows + composite actions
Marketplace Smaller, curated ⭐ Enormous
Work-item traceability ⭐ First class via Boards Issues + linking, weaker
Auth to Azure Service connection with WIF OIDC federated credential
Package feeds Artifacts Packages
Best for Enterprise governance, audit, complex release gates, existing Microsoft estates OSS, developer experience, ecosystem, GitHub-hosted code

💡 A common and sensible hybrid: code and CI in GitHub (developer experience, ecosystem), release gates and work tracking in Azure DevOps — or simply pick one and be consistent. Azure DevOps pipelines can build from a GitHub repo, and GitHub Actions can deploy to Azure just as well.

🔄 Microsoft's investment is clearly weighted toward GitHub for new features; Azure DevOps remains fully supported and is entrenched in enterprises. For a new greenfield project with no compliance constraint, GitHub Actions is the more future-proof default.

12. Troubleshooting

Symptom Cause
##[error]No hosted parallelism has been purchased or granted New organisations must request the free grant, or buy parallel jobs
Service connection auth fails after a rename The WIF subject claim sc://org/project/name no longer matches
Variable is empty in a script Secret variables must be mapped explicitly into env:
Template expression not evaluating ${{ }} is compile-time — it can't see runtime variables
A stage is skipped condition: evaluated false; remember that a dependsOn failure makes downstream conditions false unless you use always()
Artifact not found in a job Regular jobs must download explicitly; only deployment jobs auto-download
Works locally, fails on the agent Missing SDK, different OS, case-sensitive paths on Linux, or leftover state on a self-hosted agent
Intermittent failures on a self-hosted agent Dirty workspace — set workspace: clean: all

Debugging: set system.debug = true as a pipeline variable for verbose logs; download the full log archive; use - script: env | sort to dump the environment; validate YAML with the editor's built-in validation or az pipelines runs validate 🔄.

13. Checklist

  • YAML pipelines in the repo (not Classic UI pipelines)
  • Service connections use workload identity federation, not secrets
  • Separate service connections per environment, restricted to specific pipelines
  • Service connection RBAC scoped to the resource group, not the subscription
  • deployment jobs with environment: for every deploy
  • Production environment has approvals, branch control, and ideally an Azure Monitor alert check
  • Shared build/deploy logic in templates from a versioned template repo
  • Secrets in Key Vault-backed variable groups, mapped explicitly into env:
  • Build validation policy required on main, with limited bypass permissions
  • Test results and coverage published with condition: succeededOrFailed()
  • Build once; artifacts promoted through stages
  • Migrations as a separate, idempotent step before app deployment
  • postRouteTraffic verification with on.failure rollback
  • Self-hosted agents (if any) clean their workspace and are patched

🔍 Interview angles

  • job vs deployment job? Deployment jobs target an environment: approvals, checks, history, auto-download of artifacts, and deployment strategies with rollback hooks.
  • How do you authenticate a pipeline to Azure securely? Workload identity federation on the service connection — short-lived tokens, no secret to expire or rotate; subject claim is sc://org/project/connection.
  • ${{ }} vs $[ ] vs $( )? Compile-time template expansion / runtime expression before the job / runtime variable inside a step.
  • How do you enforce that every pipeline runs a security scan? Required (extends) templates at the organisation level — teams cannot bypass them by writing their own YAML.
  • How do you do zero-downtime deployment to App Service? Deploy to a staging slot, warm it up, verify health, swap, verify production, swap back on failure — all expressible in runOnce with routeTraffic/postRouteTraffic/on.failure.
  • Azure DevOps or GitHub Actions? Governance, audit and complex gates vs ecosystem and developer experience; either is defensible — say which constraint drives the choice.
